title: Predicting problem gambling among online sports and race bettors: Assessing the value of machine learning using self-reported and behavioural data
authors: Heirene, R. M.; Zhang, E.; Vanichkina, D.; Leau, C. T. de; Huynh, E. L. Y.; Gainsbury, S. M.
tldr: Machine learning models using only 30 days of behavioural betting data can adequately detect high-risk online gamblers, with performance substantially improved by adding two self-reported survey variables.
problem_and_motivation: Online gambling operators collect detailed behavioural data that could identify at-risk customers, but there is limited clarity on optimal variables, data window sufficiency, and whether short-term data enables timely risk detection under contemporary regulatory frameworks emphasising intervention. Existing studies have focused on voluntary self-exclusion as a proxy outcome and typically require 12 months of data, potentially delaying identification of at-risk customers. This study addresses these gaps by comparing 30-day versus 6-month behavioural data windows and integrating self-reported gambling risk measures.
approach: Survey data collected from 1,470 Australian online sports and race betting customers including PGSI scores and gambling satisfaction measures.
Behavioural account data provided by operator Entain covering 30-day and 6-month windows preceding survey completion.
Five machine learning algorithms compared: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Neural Network.
Three-phase experimental design: Phase 1 (30-day account data), Phase 2 (6-month account data), Phase 3 (account + survey features).
Binary classification with PGSI ≥8 threshold selected as optimal based on Phase 1 multiclass comparison results.
SMOTE applied for class imbalance; 70/30 train-test split with 10-fold cross-validation repeated five times.
findings: num: XGBoost achieved best Phase 1 AUROC of 0.752 using 30-day account data alone.
num: 6-month account-only models performed marginally worse (AUROC 0.743) than 30-day models.
num: Best overall model combined 30-day account data with survey features achieving AUROC 0.850.
num: Sensitivity ranged from 66.2% to 75.6% and specificity from 71.5% to 84.4% across optimal models.
num: Precision remained low at 32.9% to 50.5%, indicating substantial false positive rates.
Gambling satisfaction emerged as the strongest predictor in Phase 3 models (32.2% relative importance in 30-day model).
Number of active gambling accounts was the second most important survey variable (12.0% in 30-day model).
Key account-based predictors were younger age, higher deposit intensity, larger average stake, and fewer days since last bet.
Phase 4 analysis showed gambling satisfaction alone provided most of the incremental gain over account-only models.
key_figures_tables: Figure 2: Phase 1 model confusion matrix and ROC curve → XGBoost correctly identifies 66.2% high-risk with AUROC 0.752.
Figure 4: Phase 3 model with survey features → Best AUROC 0.850 with substantially improved specificity to 84.4%.
Figure 6: Incremental survey variable comparison → Gambling satisfaction alone adds most value over account-only baseline.
Table 3: All Phase 1 classification results → PGSI ≥8 with XGBoost outperforms all other model-classification combinations.
Table 4: Performance metrics across all four phases → Phase 3 models with survey features substantially outperform account-only models.

definitions.definition: Problem Gambling Severity Index, nine-item scale assessing problem gambling behaviours and adverse consequences.
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve, single-number summary of binary classification performance.
Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve, classification metric focusing on the positive class performance.
Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique, method to address class imbalance by generating synthetic minority samples.
Extreme Gradient Boosting, gradient-boosted tree algorithm providing best discriminative capacity in this study.
Index of Relative Socio-economic Advantage and Disadvantage, summary measure of social and economic conditions.
Consumer Protection Tool, operator-provided features such as deposit limits and self-exclusion.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes novel evidence that 30 days of behavioral data is sufficient for adequate gambling risk detection, challenging assumptions that extended historical windows are required. The study demonstrates that integrating minimal, non-intrusive self-reported measures substantially improves model performance beyond behavioral tracking alone. The finding that gambling satisfaction is a strong, novel predictor of risk status provides a new direction for early identification research. The paper establishes XGBoost as competitive with Random Forest for this classification task, expanding the algorithmic toolkit available for behavioral risk detection.
directly_justifies: 30-day and 6-month behavioral models perform similarly with AUROC 0.743-0.752.
Adding just two survey variables improves AUROC from 0.752 to 0.850.
Gambling satisfaction is the single strongest predictor with 32.2% relative importance.
Younger age, higher deposit intensity, and larger average stakes predict high-risk status.
Precision remains low at 33-50% indicating high false positive rates as trade-off.
limits: Account data from only two sites cannot capture cross-site gambling behavior.
Moderate sample size of 1,349-1,470 smaller than comparable studies.
Self-report bias: both predictor variables and PGSI outcome share common method variance.
Survey sample not fully representative of wider customer base due to self-selection.
PGSI self-report used as gold standard rather than clinical diagnosis.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all topic domains identified primary relevance in domains 5 (behavioral profiling) and 8 (anomaly detection), with secondary relevance in domain 12 (evaluation frameworks). Domain 5.A is highly relevant as the paper uses behavioral profiling to classify gambling risk levels. Domain 5.C is highly relevant as it compares five classification algorithms for this profiling task. Domain 8.A is moderately relevant as high-risk gambling represents anomalous spending behavior. Domain 8.B is moderately relevant as it applies multiple anomaly detection algorithms. Domain 12.A is moderately relevant through comprehensive model evaluation. Domains 1-4 (demographics, cultural practices, expense categorization, existing systems) were considered and rejected as not directly relevant to gambling risk detection. Domain 6 (forecasting) was considered but rejected as the paper focuses on classification rather than temporal prediction. Domain 7 (budget recommendation) was considered but rejected as no budget allocation logic is addressed. Domains 9-11 (mobile design, privacy, engagement) were considered and rejected as not covered. Domain 13 (savings/debt) was considered but rejected as tangential. Domain 14 (synthetic data) was considered but rejected as real data is used throughout.
limitations: Account data limited to two gambling sites cannot capture complete cross-site gambling patterns.
Sample size of 1,349-1,470 moderate compared to larger studies in the field.
Self-report bias affects both predictor and outcome variables through common method variance.
Survey sample skewed toward more engaged bettors who self-selected into participation.
PGSI self-report not validated against clinical diagnosis as the gold standard.
Precision remains low at 33-50% meaning many flagged individuals are not truly high-risk.

remember_this: XGBoost achieved best gambling risk classification with AUROC 0.752-0.850 across phases.
30 days of behavioral data performs as well as 6 months for adequate risk detection.
Gambling satisfaction is a novel and strongly predictive variable with 32.2% importance.
Just two survey variables improve model AUROC from 0.752 to 0.850 substantially.
Low precision of 33-50% indicates high false positive rates as inherent trade-off.
